issues.legal_issue: A claimant seeking partition need not obtain a declaration against an agreement for sale raised by opposing parties when the claimant denies it and the parties asserting it bear the burden of proving it.
material_facts: The claimant sought partition of property inherited by the family and denied the agreement for sale only after the opposing parties raised it in their pleadings.
The opposing parties asserted the agreement as a defence; the claimant did not seek a declaration against it.
The alleged agreement did not itself transfer ownership or create an interest in the property.
issues.conclusion: The partition suit was maintainable without a declaration against the alleged agreement for sale.
issues.legal_principle: A partition suit determines the claimant’s share, entitlement to division and separate possession, and the manner of division; the declaration sought in such a suit ordinarily concerns the claimant’s share. A document relied on by a party must be proved by that party. Under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a contract for sale does not of itself create an interest in or charge on the property. The Court relied on Controller of Estate Duty v. Kantilal Trikamlal, Shub Karan Bubna v. Sita Saran Bubna, and Bank of India v. Abhay D. Narottam.

rule.if: partition_suit and opposing_party_relies_on_sale_contract and claimant_denies_sale_contract and sale_contract_creates_no_property_interest

predicates.partition_suit: The proceeding is a suit in which a claimant seeks division and separate possession of property as a co-sharer.
predicates.opposing_party_relies_on_sale_contract: An opposing party raises a contract for sale as a basis for claiming rights affecting the property.
predicates.claimant_denies_sale_contract: The claimant denies the contract after it is raised by the opposing party.
predicates.sale_contract_creates_no_property_intere: The asserted contract for sale does not itself transfer ownership or create an interest in the property.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeking partition denies a sale contract raised by an opposing party, and the contract itself creates no property interest, the claimant may maintain the suit without seeking a declaration against the contract.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal against a decree concerning multiple co-sharers cannot proceed against surviving respondents when it has abated as to a deceased co-sharer and success could produce inconsistent decrees.
material_facts: A suit for partition resulted in a decree recognising the interests of several co-sharers and rejecting the alleged sale agreement.
The legal representatives of one respondent co-sharer were not substituted in the opposing parties’ appeal before the High Court, and the appeal abated as to that co-sharer.
The High Court nevertheless proceeded with the appeal and upheld the agreement against the surviving co-sharers, while the decree rejecting the agreement became final as to the deceased co-sharer.
issues.conclusion: The appeal had abated as to the deceased co-sharer and could not proceed against the surviving respondents; the High Court appeal was incompetent and had to be dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXII Rules 1, 2, 4(1)–(3) and 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, govern abatement and apply to appeals. Where substitution is not made within the prescribed time, an appeal abates against the deceased respondent. Under State of Punjab v. Nathu Ram, an appeal cannot proceed against remaining respondents when doing so would result in a decree inconsistent with the decree that has become final as to the deceased respondent. The Court also relied on Sardar Amarjit Singh Kalra v. Pramod Gupta and Hemareddi v. Ramachandra Yallappa Hosmani, which address whether decrees are separable and whether inconsistent decrees would result.

rule.if: appeal_from_partition_decree and respondent_co_sharer_dies and legal_representatives_not_substituted and appeal_abates_as_to_deceased and success_against_survivors_would_create_inconsistent_decrees

predicates.appeal_from_partition_decree: The proceeding is an appeal against a decree concerning the division of property among co-sharers.
predicates.respondent_co_sharer_dies: A respondent co-sharer dies while the appeal is pending.
predicates.legal_representatives_not_substituted: The deceased respondent’s legal representatives are not brought into the appeal within the required time.
predicates.appeal_abates_as_to_deceased: The appeal consequently abates as to the deceased respondent.
predicates.success_against_survivors_would_create_i: A decision for the appellant against the remaining respondents would conflict with the decree that has become final as to the deceased respondent.

issues.definition: An appeal against a partition decree cannot continue against surviving respondents if it has abated as to a deceased co-sharer and success against the survivors would conflict with the final decree concerning that co-sharer.

issues.legal_issue: A court should not uphold an alleged sale agreement when the evidence and surrounding circumstances leave its genuineness unproved, particularly where it is intertwined with a suspicious will.
material_facts: The opposing parties relied on an alleged sale agreement and a will that referred to the agreement and to the alleged seller’s debts; the courts below found the will suspicious and invalid.
The claimant denied that the agreement was genuine, leaving its proponents to prove it.
The alleged seller’s indebtedness was not supported by cogent evidence, and the evidence offered to show how the alleged purchaser raised the purchase money was unreliable.

The alleged purchaser did not obtain a registered sale deed despite the passage of time, and the explanation for the delay was inconsistent with other evidence of repayment of a loan and leasing of the property.
Neither the alleged purchaser nor the purchaser’s legal representatives sought specific performance of the agreement.
issues.conclusion: The agreement was untrustworthy and unproved; the High Court erred in upholding it, and the Trial Court’s rejection of it was restored.
issues.legal_principle: The party asserting an agreement bears the burden of proving it, and the evidence must be assessed in its full factual context. A document intertwined with a will found suspicious cannot be treated as an independent, established transaction without evaluating the relationship between the documents, the parties’ conduct, and the surrounding circumstances. The Court found the Trial Court’s assessment sound and the High Court’s contrary approach erroneous; it relied on no earlier case specifically for this evidentiary determination.

rule.if: appeal_concerning_sale_agreement_in_partition_suit and agreement_is_denied and agreement_is_intertwined_with_suspicious_will and alleged_seller_indebtedness_is_unproved and purchaser_funding_evidence_is_unreliable and delay_in_registered_transfer_is_unconvincingly_explained

predicates.appeal_concerning_sale_agreement_in_part: The proceeding is an appeal in a partition suit concerning an alleged sale agreement affecting the property claimed for partition.
predicates.agreement_is_denied: The party opposing the agreement denies that it was genuine.
predicates.agreement_is_intertwined_with_suspicious: The agreement is relied on together with a will that refers to it or to the circumstances said to explain the transaction, and the will is found suspicious.
predicates.alleged_seller_indebtedness_is_unproved: The evidence does not cogently establish the seller’s alleged debts said to explain the sale.
predicates.purchaser_funding_evidence_is_unreliable: The evidence offered to show how the purchaser obtained the purchase money is unsupported or unreliable.
predicates.delay_in_registered_transfer_is_unconvin: The purchaser did not obtain a registered transfer despite a substantial opportunity to do so, and the explanation is inconsistent with other evidence.

issues.definition: In an appeal concerning a disputed sale agreement in a partition suit, the agreement is unproved and untrustworthy when it is intertwined with a suspicious will and the asserted debts, funding, and delay explanations are not credibly established.
